meta.title: Raja Tejukayacha
meta.location: Tejukaya Mansion, Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Road, Lalbaug, Mumbai
meta.foundedNote: Explicitly dated 1967 by the 2025 artisan interview; earlier age labels are not fully consistent.
meta.intro: Raja Tejukayacha belongs to the Tejukaya Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Trust at Tejukaya Mansion, Lalbaug. Its documented story joins the Zad family of sculptors, ambitious monumental forms and an immersion tradition of carrying the idol on devotees’ shoulders. Contemporary reporting on the 2019 papier-mache idol offers a useful check against later promotional retellings. It is separate from Ganesh Galli’s Mumbaicha Raja and the Lalbaug Market mandal.

sections.title: Tejukaya Mansion and the Zad family

paragraphs.text: The 2025 interview dates the mandal to 1967 and remembers Vitthal Zad’s 14-foot idol in 1970, the Akhanda Brahmand form in 1979, Rajan Zad’s succession in 1985 and a suspended Shesh Naag composition in 2000. These are retrospective maker-history statements, not independently inspected contracts or period photographs.

sections.title: A contemporary account of paper construction

paragraphs.text: In August 2019, Mid-day interviewed Rajan Zaad and trustee Namdev Hule about a 19-by-19-foot papier-mache idol. Residents contributed newspapers, and drying the paper structure required substantial care. The trustee described shoulder-carrying as a tradition, acknowledging an exception in 1979. That contemporary account is stronger evidence for what was planned in 2019 than an undifferentiated story about an eternally unchanged idol.

A 2018 Times of India report places Tejukaya’s festival within changing Lalbaug neighborhoods. Spokesperson Rahul Dhumne said displaced residents returned in shifts and that the landlord had reserved festival space between planned towers. This is a specific account of maintaining collective activity amid redevelopment, rather than evidence that its physical surroundings stayed fixed.

For 2025, Rajan and Vidhish Zad described a warrior form and the practical challenge of drying paper in monsoon humidity. A proposed 2026 handover is a plan, not a confirmed completed succession. The trust was also named in Marathi reporting of a 2019 CPR-training programme, showing an institutional role beyond sculpture.

sections.title: Farmers, sculpture and a difficult immersion

paragraphs.text: Contemporary 2011 reporting names Rajan Zhad and representative Rahul Dhumne for a farmer-crisis tableau in which Ganesh played a dafli above a farmer's drum. A photographer's dated close-up preserves that instrument and painted surface. A November report records a remedial ritual after September immersion mishaps, including the Tejukaya idol's collapse; it preserves disputed explanations rather than a settled engineering cause.

The dated photographic sequence then shows several physical solutions: a royal throne in 2008-2010, armour beside an elephant in 2015, a four-bull carriage with farmer figures in 2016, and distinct seated throne forms in 2017-2018. The 2018 photograph carries a visible Rajan Zad sculptor plaque. Such annual evidence is stronger than treating every Tejukaya image, including the separate Matunga festival, as one interchangeable face.

sections.title: The 2019 claim and its actual awarding body

paragraphs.text: World Records India's own record entry confirms that it recorded a Tejukaya paper-Ganesh programme on 4 September 2019 and credits Rajan Vitthal Zad's conceptual design. Its 24-by-19-foot description differs from both Mid-day measurements already preserved here. The adjudicator explicitly distinguishes itself from Guinness; the later Guinness claim and full environmental performance remain unverified.

sections.title: A theme repeated after the 2011 collapse

paragraphs.text: A September 2012 preparation report records the mandal's decision to repeat the farmer-suicide theme after the previous year's interrupted immersion. Rahul Dhumne described reducing the idol from a reported 22 feet to 18 feet, with Rajan Zhad responsible for its balance. This is a contemporary statement of the next year's response; the archive does not adopt the report's shorthand as a completed investigation of the 2011 collapse.

notes.text: The 2019 report gives 19 by 19 feet; a 2025 retrospective gives different dimensions. Do not reconcile by assumption.

World Records India's own 7 Septemberentry records a 4 Septemberevent and reports 24 x 19 feet, compared with 19 x 19 in contemporary Mid-day and 22 x 18 in its 2025 retrospective. These measures are not harmonized without measurement boundaries. This establishes a World Records India claim, not a Guinness certificate.

openQuestions.title: Record organization and dimensions
openQuestions.text: World Records India now has an inspected primary publication. Obtain the measurement sheet/certificate and resolve the separate Guinness claim, rather than conflating organizations or size conventions.

openQuestions.title: When did paper construction begin?
openQuestions.text: The 2025 article mentions both a 1976 paper experiment and a first paper idol in 2019. Establish whose experiment and which idol the former describes.

openQuestions.title: Dates and artist handover
openQuestions.text: Founding-age labels differ, and a 2026 handover was only a plan in the 2025 interview. Seek dated institutional records rather than calculating a new founding date.

openQuestions.title: 2017 alternate photographer image
openQuestions.text: A Vipul Sarang frame titled Tejukaya 2017 shows a different upper-body pose from the fully framed seated 2017 Prathamesh Yeram view. It is withheld pending whether this is a secondary tableau, event assembly or miscaption.

claims.text: The festival belongs to Tejukaya Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Trust.
1967 is an explicit retrospective foundation date, with inconsistent earlier age labels.
Shoulder-carrying is described by the trustee, with an acknowledged 1979 exception.
The Guinness-record claim and exact 2019 dimensions remain unverified/conflicting.
